history.heading: Indigenous peoples and colonisation
paragraphs: Antigua and Barbuda were settled by Archaic peoples and later by Arawak-speaking and Carib (Kalinago) communities. Christopher Columbus sighted Antigua in 1493 and named it after a church in Seville.

The English established a colony on Antigua in 1632. The island became a major sugar producer worked by enslaved Africans, and Barbuda, which was leased to the Codrington family, supplied food and labour.

history.heading: Naval base and emancipation
paragraphs: English Harbour on Antigua became the main British naval base in the eastern Caribbean in the 18th century; Horatio Nelson was stationed there in the 1780s. The restored Nelson's Dockyard is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Slavery was abolished in 1834. Antigua was one of the few colonies that freed enslaved people immediately without an apprenticeship period, but the formerly enslaved remained poor and dependent on plantation work.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Trade unions and the Antigua Labour Party, led by V. C. Bird, pushed for workers' rights and self-government in the 20th century. Antigua and Barbuda became an associated state in 1967 and gained full independence on 1 November 1981, with Bird as the first prime minister.
In 2017 Hurricane Irma devastated Barbuda, forcing the evacuation of its entire population.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: The culture blends African and British influences. English is official, and Antiguan Creole is widely spoken. Carnival, held in late July and early August to commemorate emancipation, features calypso, soca and steelpan music.
The national dish is fungie (a cornmeal dish similar to polenta) and pepperpot. Antigua is said to have 365 beaches, one for every day of the year.

culture.heading: Cricket and sailing
paragraphs: Cricket is a passion; Antiguan Viv Richards is one of the greatest batsmen in history. Antigua Sailing Week is one of the Caribbean's major regattas.

politics.heading: Parliamentary monarchy
paragraphs: Antigua and Barbuda is a parliamentary democracy and a Commonwealth realm, with the British monarch as head of state represented by a governor-general. The prime minister leads the government, and Parliament has an elected House of Representatives and an appointed Senate.
Barbuda has its own council and a distinct tradition of communal land ownership, which has been the subject of disputes with the central government. There has been debate about becoming a republic.

economy.heading: Tourism and services
paragraphs: Tourism is the main source of income, employment and foreign exchange, alongside offshore financial services and a citizenship-by-investment programme. Agriculture and light manufacturing are small.
The country is highly exposed to hurricanes and to downturns in global travel. The currency is the Eastern Caribbean dollar.
